title: Day 59 · Week 8, Day 3 — Parents: the test that's about you too — carrier screening, the one in twenty-five, what your age writes into the genome, and what ten thousand couples did with the answer
summary: The fifth Parents episode, paying question three on the Day 40 sheet. Your baby is at Carnegie stage 18 (13–17 mm), the clavicle's two bone centres merging today, elbows bent, toe rays appearing — and every cell carrying a genome finished on Day 14, half hers and half yours. What a carrier is and why neither of you would know; Mendel's one in four, every pregnancy. Who is offered what: ACOG CO 690/691 (information to every pregnant woman, ideally preconception; cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy and haemoglobinopathies to all; partner tested if she's positive; any of it may be declined) and ACMG 2021 (a single ~113-condition panel for everyone, ancestry-based screening retired). The numbers: CF 1 in 2,500–3,500 white newborns, 1 in 17,000 African American, 1 in 31,000 Asian American (MedlinePlus), ~1 carrier in 25 of Northern European descent (ACOG) — and the arithmetic that closes; SMA 1 carrier in 54 pan-ethnic, 1/47 to 1/72 by ancestry, 91% detection, 1 baby in 11,000 (Sugarman 2012, 72,453 samples), the 3–4% of carriers a copy-number test misses, treatments since 2016; sickle cell trait in 1 in 13 Black babies, disease in 1 in 365 Black and 1 in 16,300 Hispanic births (CDC), screened through the CBC and electrophoresis, and the NHS programme's explicit next step: test the biological father. Fragile X (1 in 4,000 males, 1 in 8,000 females; 55–200-repeat premutations expanding only through the mother) and Tay-Sachs (1 in 30 Ashkenazi vs 1 in 300). How wide to cast the net: Haque 2016 (346,790 people; 94–392 at-risk fetuses per 100,000 by ancestry; guideline panels catching 6–87% of what the expanded panel finds). What a result does to a couple: Mackenzie's Mission (Kirk 2024, NEJM; 10,038 couples, ≥1,281 genes; 1.9% newly at increased chance; 76.6% used or planned an intervention; more anxiety, low regret, 98.9% acceptability). The father's share: ~2 new mutations per year of paternal age (Kong 2012, 78 trios), autism RR 5.75 for fathers ≥40 (Reichenberg 2006) and 1.66 for fathers ≥50 vs twenties in 5.77 million children (Sandin 2016) — about 1 in 190 moving toward 1 in 110. And your blood type: Rh D negative in ~15% of Europeans (ACOG PB 181), anti-D prevention (MedlinePlus), and the 373,300 cases of Rh disease still occurring worldwide in 2010 (Bhutani 2013).
action: Fifteen minutes tonight, together, with the Day 40 question sheet. One: decide whether you want carrier screening and, if so, ask for both of you to be tested at once — rewrite question three as 'We'd like carrier screening; which panel do you offer, can we both be tested now, and how long do results take?' Two: put both family-history sheets side by side; note anything that recurs on either side, any ancestry that puts a condition on the list, and any blood relation between the two of you. Three: write your blood type next to hers under question six, or the plan to find it out this week. Then say one sentence out loud before folding the sheet: 'If we're both carriers of something, here's roughly what we'd want to do.' You don't have to agree tonight; you have to have started.
